title: USIPHU Pilot Question Bank — General Surgery
description: Pilot set derived from user-provided examination papers. Editorially checked against open-access references; all items remain draft pending source-page visual confirmation and qualified clinical/faculty sign-off.
source_policy: Preserve candidate provenance and do not infer official past-paper answer keys. Editorial answer proposals are independently evidence-checked and are not faculty-approved.

questions.stem: Which clinical finding on breast examination is more suggestive of malignancy than a benign breast lesion?
options: Fixation or tethering to underlying pectoral structures
Variation in size through the menstrual cycle
questions.explanation: A mass fixed to the skin or chest wall/pectoral structures is a concerning feature for malignancy. Mobility and cyclical variation are more often associated with benign lesions, although no single examination feature establishes the diagnosis.

evidence_sources.title: New Palpable Breast Mass
evidence_sources.supports: Describes inspection for tethering to underlying structures and the need for structured clinical assessment; fixed masses are concerning.

editorial_notes: Option C clarified from 'tethering to underlying muscular structures' to distinguish fixation/tethering from skin dimpling.
questions.jurisdiction: International evidence; local faculty review required

questions.stem: What is the most common site of distant metastasis in breast cancer?
questions.explanation: Bone is a common and the most frequent distant metastatic site listed for breast cancer in the NCI overview. The pattern of spread varies with tumour biology and subtype.

evidence_sources.title: Metastatic Cancer: When Cancer Spreads
evidence_sources.supports: Lists bone, brain, liver and lung as common metastatic sites for breast cancer, with bone listed first.

questions.jurisdiction: International evidence; local faculty review required

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a new painless, hard breast lump. Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
questions.explanation: For a woman aged 40 years or older with a palpable breast mass, diagnostic mammography (or diagnostic tomosynthesis) is usually appropriate as initial imaging. Ultrasound may be added depending on the findings; biopsy is guided by the imaging and clinical assessment.

evidence_sources.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Palpable Breast Masses
evidence_sources.supports: For adult women aged 40 or older with a palpable breast mass, diagnostic mammography/tomosynthesis is usually appropriate initial imaging.

editorial_notes: Stem changed from 'most appropriate next investigation' to 'initial imaging investigation' to avoid conflating imaging with tissue diagnosis.
Option C specified as diagnostic mammography; ultrasound may be complementary.
questions.source_title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Palpable Breast Masses
questions.jurisdiction: International evidence; local faculty review required

questions.stem: After modified radical mastectomy, a patient develops medial scapular winging and weakness of shoulder movement. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior. Injury causes serratus anterior palsy and medial scapular winging, and may impair shoulder elevation/abduction.

evidence_sources.title: Long-term Improvements of Neuroplasty and Scalene Muscle Resection in LTN-injured Winged Scapula Patients
evidence_sources.publisher: Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open
evidence_sources.supports: Describes long thoracic nerve injury as a cause of scapular winging and impaired shoulder movement.

editorial_notes: Minor grammar correction only; options retained.

questions.stem: The three surgical levels of axillary lymph nodes are defined in relation to which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation: Berg levels I, II and III are defined by the position of axillary nodes relative to pectoralis minor: lateral/inferior, behind, and medial/superior to the muscle, respectively.

evidence_sources.title: Sonographic localisation of lymph nodes suspicious of metastatic breast cancer to surgical axillary levels
evidence_sources.supports: Describes the three surgical axillary levels relative to pectoralis minor.

questions.source_title: Sonographic localisation of lymph nodes suspicious of metastatic breast cancer to surgical axillary levels

questions.stem: Which is the most common benign cause of spontaneous bloody nipple discharge from a single duct?
questions.explanation: Intraductal papilloma is a common and often the most frequent benign cause of pathological nipple discharge, including bloody single-duct discharge. Duct ectasia is another important benign cause; malignancy must still be excluded.

evidence_sources.title: Nipple discharge: The state of the art
evidence_sources.supports: Defines pathological discharge and reports intraductal papilloma and duct ectasia as common benign causes; papilloma is frequent in single-duct bloody discharge.

editorial_notes: Stem narrowed to benign cause of pathological single-duct discharge; malignancy remains an important differential and requires assessment.
questions.source_title: Nipple discharge: The state of the art
questions.jurisdiction: International evidence; local faculty review required

questions.stem: Which is the most frequent histological type of breast carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Invasive ductal carcinoma (also termed invasive carcinoma of no special type in contemporary classification) is the most common histological type of breast cancer. Invasive lobular carcinoma is the next most common major type.

evidence_sources.title: Breast Cancer Treatment (PDQ®) — Histopathological Classification
evidence_sources.supports: States invasive ductal cancer is the most common histological type, comprising approximately 70–80% of cases.

editorial_notes: Terminology modernized from 'infiltrating ductal' to 'invasive ductal'; option meaning retained.
questions.jurisdiction: International evidence; local faculty review required

questions.stem: Which clinical presentation is characteristic of mammary Paget disease?
options: A mass beneath the nipple without skin change
A unilateral red, scaly eczematous nipple lesion
questions.explanation: Mammary Paget disease typically presents as a unilateral eczematous or psoriasiform lesion of the nipple-areolar complex and is frequently associated with underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma. Diagnosis requires biopsy; management depends on associated breast pathology.

evidence_sources.title: Paget Disease of the Nipple
evidence_sources.supports: Describes unilateral eczematous-to-psoriasiform plaque of nipple/areola associated with underlying ductal carcinoma.

editorial_notes: Terminology and stem clarified; source's 'unilateral red scaly nipple' option preserved in meaning.
questions.jurisdiction: International evidence; local faculty review required
